slides.sub: An unfair coin holds less. That sentence is the whole field.

slides.quote: A coin that always lands heads tells you nothing when it lands heads.
slides.text: Surprise is the thing to measure. An event of probability `p` carries `-log2 p` bits of it -- rare means surprising.

slides.text: Entropy peaks at the fair coin and dies at both walls. The certain coin surprises no one, so it informs no one.
Same coin, different bias. The 90/10 coin pays less than half a bit per flip -- predictability is a discount.
slides.note: Labels show two decimals; the bars use the full value.

slides.text: Entropy is the average of `-log2 p`, weighted by `p`. Three lines, base two, answer in bits.
lines: return -sum(p * math.log2(p) for p in ps if p)
slides.note: Guard the `if p`: log2(0) is not a number you want.

slides.text: Uniform over N outcomes holds log2 N bits. Each bit is one yes-or-no question that halves the search.
slides.note: Eight doors, three questions, always enough.

slides.quote: Entropy says how uncertain you are, never what it costs you. The bit does not know what it is about.
slides.text: Same math for a coin and a catastrophe. Importance lives outside the formula -- which is why compression uses it and decisions cannot.
Linear algebra, calculus and probability from the axioms up -- one log at a time, in public.

caption:
A coin that always lands heads tells you nothing. That is not philosophy, it is arithmetic.

Surprise is -log2 p and entropy is its average. A fair coin pays a full bit per flip, a 90/10 coin pays 0.47, a certain one pays nothing.

And bits are questions: 8 doors need 3 yes-or-no questions, 32 need 5.

The catch: entropy never knows what the bit is about. Same math for a coin and a catastrophe.

What is the most lopsided probability you deal with daily?
